title: How this nvim config actually boots

steps.title: Seven requires, in order
steps.note: Seven requires, run top to bottom, and that order is the whole boot sequence. Two of them are load-bearing in ways the file does not say out loud. `keymaps` has to be first because it sets `mapleader`. And `lazy-init` has to come before line 8, because which-key is a plugin: `require("which-key")` only resolves once lazy has put it on the runtimepath. Move line 5 below line 8 and startup breaks with a module-not-found.

steps.title: Leader before every mapping
steps.note: Why keymaps goes first. `mapleader` is read when a mapping is *created*, not when the key is pressed, so anything bound to `<leader>x` before line 3 would silently end up on `\x`. Every plugin spec under lua/plugins defines leader mappings, and lazy reads all of them one line later in init.lua. Line 2 maps space to <Nop> so the old space-is-right-arrow motion stops fighting the leader.

steps.title: The re-source guard
steps.note: The entire file sits inside a global guard. That means `:source $MYVIMRC` re-runs keymaps, lsp and options but deliberately skips lazy, because `lazy.setup()` is not idempotent: a second call re-registers every spec. Inside the guard is the standard self-bootstrap, git-cloning lazy.nvim into stdpath('data') on a machine that has never run this config. It is the only network call in the boot path, and only on first run.

steps.title: Two importers, not a list
steps.note: Prepend, not append, so lazy sits ahead of $VIMRUNTIME. Then `setup` gets two importers rather than a list of plugins: `import = "plugins"` means require every file directly under lua/plugins and treat what it returns as a spec. Directly under. Import is not recursive, which is why lua/plugins/lsp needs its own entry, and why a spec file dropped into a deeper subdirectory would be silently ignored.

steps.title: A spec file is just data
steps.note: A spec file returns either one spec or a list; this one returns two. Because of the import above, this table is *built* on every single launch. That is fine, it is just data. What gets deferred is the `config` function further down. Conflating the two is the usual reason a lazy-loaded config still feels slow at startup.

steps.title: cond drops the plugin
steps.note: The one piece of conditional loading in the config, and it resolves at spec-build time. `vim.env.HERDR_ENV` is read the instant this file is required, against the environment nvim inherited from the shell that launched it. So herdr-splits is present inside herdr and *absent* outside it. Not deferred, absent: lazy drops the plugin, its config, and its eight <C-hjkl>/<M-hjkl> keymaps. Line 7's `event = 'VeryLazy'` only decides when a plugin that already passed `cond` loads. If <C-h> does nothing in an nvim you started by hand, this line is the reason, and `:Lazy load` will not rescue that session.

steps.title: The twin that always loads
steps.note: The second spec in the same file, and it has no `cond`. herdr-nvim, the annotate-lines-and-send-them-to-the-agent side, loads everywhere. herdr-splits, the pane navigation side, only loads inside herdr. Two plugins with confusingly similar names and deliberately different lifecycles, which is worth remembering when something herdr-shaped works in one nvim and not another.

steps.title: Servers probed, not installed
steps.note: Back on the init.lua path, line 6. There is no mason and no installer anywhere in this config. It probes $PATH with `executable()` and enables only the servers whose binary is actually installed. A missing binary is a silent no-op rather than a startup error, which is exactly why this file behaves differently on the work machine and the personal one. This runs after lazy.setup, so anything a plugin has already done to `vim.lsp` is in place by now.

steps.title: lsp/ is not lua/
steps.note: `vim.lsp.enable("lua_ls")` takes no config table. It goes looking for `lsp/lua_ls.lua` on the runtimepath, and lands here. Note the directory: `lsp/` is a sibling of `lua/`, not inside it, because runtimepath lookup and `require()` are different mechanisms that happen to both start at the config root. That is the whole nvim 0.11 convention. Adding a language server to this config is one line in the table you just saw plus one file in this directory.

steps.title: Folds open, treesitter folds
steps.note: Options run last, after lazy and after LSP. `foldlevel` and `foldlevelstart` at 99 mean folds start open instead of the whole file collapsing the moment you open it, which is the usual first complaint about treesitter folding. The FileType autocmd below then hands folding to `vim.treesitter.foldexpr()` for every filetype at once through `opt_local`, which is why there is no per-language fold configuration anywhere in this repo. Also worth noticing while you are here: this file is indented with tabs and almost nothing else in the config is.

steps.title: Required for side effects
steps.note: Last stop: init.lua lines 9 and 10. These two requires are not plugin specs and their return value is thrown away. They are required purely for side effects, and this file's payload is these bottom seven lines, registering two user commands at startup. navgame.lua does the same thing with `:NavGame`. So the real cost of a cold boot here is: leader, lazy (which reads every file under lua/plugins), an executable probe per language server, options, and a handful of `nvim_create_user_command` calls. Everything else in the config is deferred behind a lazy event or an autocmd.
